paper_name: Removing Cost Volumes from Optical Flow Estimators

sections.abstract: Cost volumes are a standard component in modern optical flow estimators, but their high computational and space complexity often limits processing speed and input resolution. This paper observes that cost volumes lose their importance once other network components, such as those in a RAFT-based pipeline, have been sufficiently trained. The authors introduce a training strategy that allows for the removal of cost volumes during inference, leading to significantly improved speeds and reduced memory requirements. Three models are proposed: ReCoVEr-CX, ReCoVEr-RN, and ReCoVEr-MN. ReCoVEr-CX achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while being $1.2\times$ faster and having a $6\times$ lower memory footprint than comparable models. ReCoVEr-MN can process Full HD frames at 20 FPS using only 500 MB of GPU memory.
sections.introduction: Optical flow estimation is a fundamental task for applications like video inpainting and object tracking. Modern deep learning methods use 'cost volumes' (correlation layers or cross-attention) to measure pixel similarity, but these suffer from quadratic growth in complexity, $O(h^2w^2)$, relative to input resolution. For example, in SEA-RAFT, the cost volume accounts for over half of the computations, and processing Full HD (1920 $\times$ 1080) frames requires 4 GB for the cost volume alone, growing to 62 GB if resolution is doubled. The authors propose a method to adapt networks during training so that the cost volume is no longer required at inference time.
sections.method: The authors propose ReCoVEr, focusing on RAFT-based architectures like SEA-RAFT. While early methods used optimization or CNNs with correlation layers, recent architectures use cost volumes or cross-attention with $O(h^2w^2)$ complexity. Some methods reduce this to $O(D^2hw)$ using fixed search ranges or pyramids. ReCoVEr removes these volumes entirely for inference. The strategy involves a 'cut-off' or 'fade-out' approach where the cost volume contribution is removed after initial training. Three context network backbones are utilized: ReCoVEr-RN (ResNet-34), ReCoVEr-CX (ConvNeXt-t), and ReCoVEr-MN (MobileNetV3-L), providing feature maps at $1/8$ resolution. Technical implementation involves modifying the refinement network to receive all-zero tensors after the cut-off point, simplifying the removal of the feature network.
sections.experiments: The training protocol involves sequential stages: TartanAir, FlyingChairs, FlyingThings, and a final TSKH combination (Sintel, KITTI, and HD1K). The 'cut-off' strategy is implemented during the FlyingThings stage. Models are evaluated against state-of-the-art methods including SEA-RAFT, GMA, and GMFlow. The study also evaluates downsample-upsample strategies, finding their accuracy benefits inconsistent across datasets like Sintel and Spring, which justifies the focus on architectural removal.
sections.results: ReCoVEr-CX achieves an EPE of 0.51 on the Spring dataset, surpassing SEA-RAFT (0.54) while being $1.2\times$ faster and using $6\times$ less memory. ReCoVEr-RN is $2.5\times$ faster than RAFT with $1/8$ the memory. ReCoVEr-MN is the most efficient, requiring only 0.49 GB of memory. Qualitatively, ReCoVEr-CX yields sharper motion boundaries and better foreground separation. Supplementary analysis confirms that ReCoVEr models scale significantly better than SEA-RAFT across resolutions (Figs. A.1, A.2) and provides additional visual results from DAVIS, KITTI, Sintel, and Spring.
sections.conclusion: The authors demonstrate that cost volumes, while essential for learning pixel similarities initially, can be removed for inference without sacrificing accuracy. The resulting models provide efficient high-resolution optical flow. Limitations include ReCoVEr-MN's performance on large motions and textureless regions, and the diminishing efficiency of MobileNetV3 at extreme resolutions. Future work will investigate applying these strategies to other refinement architectures.
sections.supplementary: The supplementary material provides further technical details, clarifying that FLOPS reduction translates directly to runtime improvements. It includes comprehensive runtime and memory scaling comparisons across various resolutions and additional qualitative examples (Figs. A.3 and A.4) demonstrating robust performance across diverse scenes.
